experiment.rationale:
Five experts with a wide validity spread (0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.62, 0.55) make the cue hierarchy salient, so Take The Best (TTB) has an unambiguous search order, while Tallying is indifferent to that order. The 12 unique pairs (repeated 8x each, ~96 trials) fall into three families, all of which dissociate the two models.

(1) Direct-conflict pairs (T1-T6, T11-T12): one option wins the highest discriminating cue while the other wins the majority of the remaining lower-validity cues. TTB predicts choice of the top-cue winner on every one of these; Tallying predicts the opposite option. Critically, the tally margin is parametrically varied: margin 3 (T1/T2: 1 vs 4 cue wins), margin 2 (T5/T6: 1 vs 3; T11/T12: 1 vs 3 with the top cue tied so TTB's deciding cue is expert 2), and margin 1 (T3/T4: 2 vs 3). This yields the key *quantitative* dissociation: TTB's softmax operates on a binary 1/0 score, so its predicted choice probability for the top-cue winner is identical (sigmoid(beta), lapse-corrected) across all conflict trials regardless of tally margin, whereas Tallying's softmax probability grows monotonically with the tally margin (exp(beta*1) vs exp(beta*2) vs exp(beta*3) contrasts). Thus a flat, margin-invariant preference for the top-cue winner is uniquely TTB, while a graded, margin-increasing preference for the majority-cue winner is uniquely Tallying.

(2) Tally-tie pairs (T7-T10): the two options split cue wins evenly (1-1 or 2-2), so Tallying is forced to guess at exactly 50/50 irrespective of its parameters, while TTB still decides confidently via the highest discriminating cue. Systematic above-chance choice of the top-cue winner here cannot be produced by Tallying under any beta/epsilon, making these trials a parameter-free falsification test.

(3) Left/right and direction counterbalancing: every conflict and tie configuration appears in both A-favoring and B-favoring versions, so any side bias cancels and cannot masquerade as evidence for either heuristic.

T11/T12 additionally probe whether the deciding cue must be the very best cue: expert 1 ties, so TTB's decision rests on expert 2 while the tally strongly favors the other option; this separates TTB from any 'only-the-single-best-cue-matters' caricature as well as from Tallying.

metric.rationale: The design contains four trial types (T7-T10) on which the two options split feature-wise wins exactly evenly (1-1 or 2-2), so the Tallying softmax is mathematically uniform for ANY beta and epsilon: Tallying must choose the highest-validity-cue winner exactly 50% of the time, with only binomial noise (32 such trials per subject => between-subject SD ~0.09). Take The Best, in contrast, resolves these pairs on the first discriminating cue and therefore chooses the top-cue winner with probability (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which for essentially the whole plausible parameter range sits well above chance (~0.80-0.95). The metric is the proportion of tally-tie trials on which the option favored by the highest-validity discriminating cue was chosen. It is parameter-free for Tallying (fixed at 0.5, tight across subjects) and clearly above 0.5 for TTB, giving a large mean gap with modest per-subject variability. It also works identically on a single subject's slice and on the pooled data, and side/direction counterbalancing in the design ensures response bias cannot inflate it.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by consulting cues one at a time in order of validity, stopping at the first cue that discriminates between the two options. That cue alone determines the choice: the option with the higher value on the discriminating cue wins, and no other cue is consulted. Cues with lower validity are never reached when a higher-validity cue already discriminates, so Take The Best is a "one-reason" decision rule — only a single feature is ever used on any given choice. Because only the sign of the comparison on the top discriminating cue matters, TTB ignores both the magnitude of that difference and all information on lower-validity cues, making it maximally frugal in the use of evidence. Cue validities are subjective and can be learned, inferred from instructions, or fixed by task structure. When no cue discriminates (all feature-wise comparisons tie) the learner has no basis for preference and must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the binary TTB score (winner = 1, loser = 0) with inverse temperature beta, plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Take The Best (Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996).
    # Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors for the current
    # trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features), row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B. Cue cascade: features are consulted in order
    # of descending validity; the first discriminating cue (strict
    # inequality) determines the winner; if no cue discriminates,
    # the model guesses uniformly. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"TTB expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )
    n_features = stim.shape[1]

    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )
    # Descending validity; argsort is stable so validity ties break
    # toward the earlier feature index.
    cue_order = np.argsort(-val, kind="stable").tolist()

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    winner = None
    for j in cue_order:
        if a[j] > b[j]:
            winner = 0
            break
        if b[j] > a[j]:
            winner = 1
            break

    if winner is None:
        # No discriminating cue — pure guess.
        return np.ones(2) / 2.0

    scores = np.array([1.0, 0.0]) if winner == 0 else np.array([0.0, 1.0])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. For the
    # binary TTB score this collapses to sigmoid(beta) for the winner,
    # giving a direct mapping from beta onto the paper's flip-noise
    # levels (beta=0 ↔ 50/50; beta ≫ 1 ↔ deterministic).
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

experiment.rationale:
Goal: dissociate Tallying (advocated) from Take The Best by factorially crossing (i) which option wins the highest-validity discriminating cue \u2014 the only thing TTB is sensitive to \u2014 with (ii) the tally margin, the only thing Tallying is sensitive to. Six experts with a wide, deliberately scrambled validity spread [0.93, 0.57, 0.79, 0.86, 0.62, 0.71] give the descending cue order f0 > f3 > f2 > f5 > f4 > f1, so validity rank is decoupled from screen position (unlike a monotone left-to-right layout, this prevents a positional-ordering confound from mimicking TTB).

Core manipulation (trials 1,3,5,7,9 and their exact A/B mirrors 2,4,6,8,10): option A always wins expert f0 (validity .93), so TTB's deciding cue and predicted winner are IDENTICAL across all five cells; its predicted P(choose A) is the constant (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 regardless of the rest of the profile. Meanwhile the tally margin is parametrically swept M = -3, -1, 0, +2, +4 by re-allocating the five lower-validity cues. Tallying's softmax gives P(A) = sigmoid(beta*M) (lapse-corrected), i.e. a strictly monotone, sign-crossing psychometric function of M: strong B-preference at M=-3, weak B at M=-1, exactly 50/50 at M=0, and increasingly strong A at +2 and +4. A flat line across the five margin cells is a unique TTB signature; a monotone increasing line crossing chance at M=0 is a unique Tallying signature. Crucially the design contains both conflict cells (M=-3, -1: TTB says A, Tallying says B) and agreement cells (M=+2, +4: both say A), so the same subject's data pin down beta from the agreement cells and then test whether the conflict cells reverse (Tallying) or not (TTB) \u2014 a within-subject, parameter-anchored test rather than a mere direction contrast.

Tally-tie cells (trials 5, 6): three cue wins each. Tallying MUST be exactly 50/50 for every possible beta and epsilon, while TTB confidently picks the f0 winner. Systematic above-chance choice here parameter-free falsifies Tallying; chance performance parameter-free falsifies TTB.

Low-rank deciding cue (trials 11, 12): the two best experts (f0=.93 and f3=.86) are tied, so TTB must descend to f2 (.79), which favors A, while the tally favors B by 2 (B wins f5, f4, f1). This checks whether the one-reason rule really cascades down the validity hierarchy or whether subjects instead aggregate the three lower experts \u2014 an independent conflict test whose TTB prediction is the same magnitude as in trials 1/3 (binary score) but whose Tallying prediction is intermediate (|M|=2).

Every configuration appears in both an A-favoring and a B-favoring mirror, so side bias cancels exactly and cannot masquerade as support for either heuristic. Tie cues are encoded sometimes as 0-0 and sometimes as 1-1 to prevent a 'count the 1s' surface strategy from being confounded with either model. 12 unique pairs \u00d7 8 repetitions \u2248 96 trials.

metric.rationale:
The design contains conflict trials in which the tally winner and the one-reason (TTB) winner are opposite options, and where the tally margin is large (|M| >= 2): trials 1/2 (A wins the .93 expert but loses the tally 1-4) and trials 11/12 (the two best experts tie so TTB descends to f2 and picks one option, while the tally favors the other by 2). This metric is the proportion of choices on exactly those trials that agree with the tally winner.

Prediction under Tallying: with margin magnitude 2-3, softmax choice is near-deterministic for the tally winner for almost the whole beta range, so the score is (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*|M|)+eps/2, i.e. near 0.85-1.0. Prediction under TTB: exactly the complement, eps/2 + (1-eps)*(1-sigmoid(beta)), i.e. near 0-0.15. The expected mean gap is ~0.7-0.75 while per-subject variance is small (only lapse-rate spread plus binomial noise over 32 trials at extreme p), which is what Welch's test at N=25 needs. Restricting to |M| >= 2 avoids the weak M=1 cells where Tallying's own prediction is soft; excluding agreement and tie cells removes trials where the two theories predict the same thing and which would only dilute the contrast.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by counting, across all features, how often one option has a higher value than the other. The option that wins on more features is chosen. Tallying discards cardinal magnitudes — only the sign of each feature-wise comparison matters — so the heuristic is robust to monotone rescaling of individual features and cannot be swayed by a single large feature difference in the way Equal-Weight can. Ties on an individual feature contribute nothing to either count: that cue is simply treated as uninformative for the pair. No feature is privileged, in contrast to Take The Best; every cue contributes equally to the tally. When the two counts are equal the heuristic has no basis for preference and the learner must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the two tallies with inverse temperature beta (interpolating between fully deterministic choice at large beta and uniform guessing at beta = 0), plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.

def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Tallying heuristic (Dawes 1979; Gigerenzer &
    # Goldstein 1999). Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors
    # for the current trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features),
    # with row 0 = option A, row 1 = option B. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Tallying expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    # Count strict feature-wise wins; ties contribute to neither option.
    a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
    b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
    scores = np.array([a_wins, b_wins])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. When
    # a_wins == b_wins the softmax is exactly uniform regardless of
    # beta, which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating
    # tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

next_theory.description:
**Limited-Sample Noisy Cue Counting (LSNC).** People neither integrate all cues (Tallying) nor consult a single best cue (Take-The-Best). Instead, on each choice they inspect only a *limited, randomly selected subset* of the presented expert ratings, tally feature-wise wins **within that sample only**, and pick the option that is ahead in the sample; a within-sample tie (including a sample containing no discriminating cue) forces a guess.

Three commitments define the theory:
1. **Equal-probability sampling.** The inspected subset is drawn uniformly at random from the whole profile — it is *not* validity-ordered and *not* validity-weighted. Stated validities are too weakly represented to steer the search order, so no cue enjoys priority. Consequently, on globally tally-tied, side-counterbalanced profiles the process is exactly symmetric and choice is 50/50, with no tendency to follow the most valid discriminating cue.
2. **Sample-size limitation with tie dilution.** The number of cues actually inspected, K, is a random variable with mean k < n (implemented as K = 1 + Binomial(n−1, q), so at least one cue is always read). Because the subset is drawn from *all* features, non-discriminating (tied) features occupy sampling slots and dilute the evidence: two profiles with the same raw tally margin M produce different adherence depending on how many uninformative cues pad the profile, and on the proportion (not the raw count) of informative cues won. This is the signature that dissociates LSNC from softmax Tallying, whose predictions depend only on M.
3. **Encoding noise + lapse.** Each inspected feature-wise comparison is registered with the wrong sign with probability nu (attention/encoding noise), and with probability epsilon the whole decision is replaced by a coin flip.

Because a small, noisy sample can easily reverse the sign of a large global margin, adherence to the full-tally winner is *capped well below 1* even on high-margin conflict trials — the systematic attenuation that full Tallying cannot produce without degenerate temperature — while symmetry guarantees exactly chance behaviour on tally-tied pairs.

def predict(parameters, state, history):
    import numpy as np
    from math import comb

    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError("LSNC expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape %s." % (stim.shape,))
    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    n = int(a.shape[0])

    nA = int(np.sum(a > b))          # cues on which A wins
    nB = int(np.sum(b > a))          # cues on which B wins
    nT = n - nA - nB                 # uninformative (tied) cues

    k = float(parameters["k"])            # mean number of cues inspected
    nu = float(parameters["nu"])          # per-comparison encoding error
    eps = float(parameters["epsilon"])    # lapse rate
    nu = float(min(max(nu, 0.0), 0.5))
    eps = float(min(max(eps, 0.0), 1.0))

    if n == 0:
        return np.ones(2) / 2.0

    # ---- distribution of the inspected sample size K in {1..n} -------------
    if n == 1:
        pK = np.array([1.0])
    else:
        q = (k - 1.0) / (n - 1.0)
        q = float(min(max(q, 0.0), 1.0))
        pK = np.array([comb(n - 1, s - 1) * (q ** (s - 1)) * ((1.0 - q) ** (n - s))
                       for s in range(1, n + 1)], dtype=float)
        tot = pK.sum()
        pK = pK / tot if tot > 0 else np.ones(n) / float(n)

    # ---- exact enumeration over sample compositions ------------------------
    pA = 0.0
    for si, s in enumerate(range(1, n + 1)):
        w = float(pK[si])
        if w <= 0.0:
            continue
        denom = float(comb(n, s))
        for ai in range(0, min(nA, s) + 1):
            for bi in range(0, min(nB, s - ai) + 1):
                ti = s - ai - bi
                if ti < 0 or ti > nT:
                    continue
                cnt = comb(nA, ai) * comb(nB, bi) * comb(nT, ti)
                if cnt == 0:
                    continue
                ph = float(cnt) / denom          # multivariate hypergeometric
                m = ai + bi                      # informative cues in sample
                if m == 0:
                    pA += w * ph * 0.5           # nothing discriminates -> guess
                    continue
                # X = number of sampled comparisons REGISTERED as A-wins
                d1 = np.array([comb(ai, x) * ((1.0 - nu) ** x) * (nu ** (ai - x))
                               for x in range(ai + 1)], dtype=float)
                d2 = np.array([comb(bi, x) * (nu ** x) * ((1.0 - nu) ** (bi - x))
                               for x in range(bi + 1)], dtype=float)
                dist = np.convolve(d1, d2)
                xs = np.arange(m + 1)
                p_win = float(dist[2 * xs > m].sum())
                p_tie = float(dist[2 * xs == m].sum())
                pA += w * ph * (p_win + 0.5 * p_tie)

    pA = float(min(max(pA, 0.0), 1.0))
    p = np.array([pA, 1.0 - pA], dtype=float)
    p = (1.0 - eps) * p + eps * 0.5
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1.0)
    return p / p.sum()
next_theory.rationale:
Take-The-Best (pi_1) is falsified in both directions (0.90 vs 0.474; 0.14 vs 0.65) and softmax Tallying (pi_2), while parameter-freely correct at chance on Experiment 1's tally ties, over-predicts conflict-trial adherence (0.85 vs 0.65) because a large raw margin drives its softmax to near-determinism unless beta collapses toward guessing everywhere. LSNC dissolves this tension with a single mechanism.

(1) **Experiment 1 is fit parameter-freely.** On tally-tied, side-counterbalanced profiles nA = nB, and uniform (validity-blind) subset sampling plus symmetric encoding noise make the whole process exchangeable in A/B, so p(A) = 0.5 exactly for every parameter setting. Predicted TTB-agreement = 0.50 (real 0.4738), and the only across-subject variance is binomial (0.25/32 ≈ 0.0078 vs. observed 0.0073) — matching not just the mean but the observed between-subject spread.

(2) **Experiment 2's attenuation falls out mechanically.** The two conflict configurations are (nA=1, nB=4, nT=1) and (nA=1, nB=3, nT=2). Exact enumeration gives adherence to the tally winner of ~0.60 (K=1), ~0.63 (K=2), ~0.67 (K=3) at nu ≈ 0.25, rising only slowly toward 1 as K → n. With the declared ranges (mean k ≈ 2.5, nu ≈ 0.22, eps ≈ 0.06) the pooled prediction is ≈ 0.655, essentially the observed 0.6538, and the parameter spread contributes ≈ 0.002 on top of the 0.007 binomial variance, landing near the observed 0.0092. Crucially, adherence is *capped*: no amount of increasing determinism drives it to 1 unless the sample becomes the full profile, so the model is not merely a re-tuned Tallying.

(3) **It is a genuine rival with a testable dissociation.** Because the subset is drawn from all cues — including tied ones — adherence depends on the *proportion* of informative cues won and is *diluted* by uninformative cues, not on the raw margin M. Note above that the 1-vs-4 (margin 3, one tied cue) and 1-vs-3 (margin 2, two tied cues) cases already differ by ~0.03–0.05 at fixed parameters in a direction Tallying cannot represent; a 2-0 versus 4-2 design (both M=2) yields a large predicted gap under LSNC and none under Tallying. The model uses no validity information at all, honouring the Experiment 1 evidence against validity-ordered or validity-weighted search, and it generalises to any n_features and any validity vector without refitting.

experiment.rationale:
GOAL: dissociate Limited-Sample Noisy Cue Counting (LSNC, advocated) from softmax Tallying (competing). Tallying's choice probability is a function of the tally margin M = nA - nB ALONE: any two pairs with the same M must produce exactly the same P(choose A) for every possible beta and epsilon. LSNC instead depends on the full composition (nA, nB, nT): tied/uninformative cues occupy sampling slots (tie dilution) and only the PROPORTION of sampled informative cues won matters, so two profiles with identical M but different numbers of tied cues yield different adherence. The design is therefore a 3 (margin: M = 1, 2, 3) x 2 (informative density: SPARSE, all discriminating cues won by one option but many tied cues; DENSE, no/few tied cues but the loser also wins several cues) factorial, fully mirrored for side. Tallying predicts a pure main effect of margin and EXACTLY ZERO density effect (parameter-free); LSNC predicts sparse > dense at every margin.

CELLS (A-favouring version; the mirror swaps A and B):
- S1 sparse M=+1: (nA,nB,nT) = (1,0,5)
- D1 dense  M=+1: (3,2,1)
- S2 sparse M=+2: (2,0,4)
- D2 dense  M=+2: (4,2,0)
- S3 sparse M=+3: (3,0,3)
- D3 dense  M=+3: (4,1,1)

QUANTITATIVE LSNC PREDICTIONS (k=2.5, nu=0.20, epsilon=0, exact enumeration of the hypergeometric sample compositions): M=1: 0.625 (sparse) vs 0.572 (dense); M=2: 0.702 vs 0.630; M=3: 0.754 vs 0.707. So LSNC predicts a ~5-7 point sparse-minus-dense advantage at EVERY margin (and the gap grows with k), while adherence stays capped well below 1 even at M=3. Tallying predicts 0 at every margin. Aggregated over the 3 margins each subject contributes 48 sparse and 48 dense trials, so the parameter-free density contrast is powerfully estimated within subject.

CONFOUND CONTROL (critical): (i) In every A-favouring cell option A wins the highest-validity discriminating cue f0 (0.92), which also discriminates in every cell, so Take-The-Best (or any 'best cue' strategy) predicts a CONSTANT P(A) across all six cells and cannot generate a density effect. (ii) Validity-weighted additive evidence (log-odds weights w = [2.44, 0.41, 1.59, 0.90, 0.20, 1.21]) was deliberately matched between the sparse and dense member of each margin pair: M=1: +2.44 vs +2.13; M=2: +2.64 vs +2.53; M=3: +3.05 vs +3.16. Hence a WADD-type subject also cannot produce the sparse>dense pattern; only sample-limited counting with tie dilution can. (iii) Validity order is scrambled relative to screen position (descending order is f0, f2, f5, f3, f1, f4) so positional heuristics do not mimic validity-ordered search. (iv) Tied cues are encoded sometimes as 1-1 and sometimes as 0-0 so that the number of displayed 1s is not a constant cue to density. (v) Every configuration appears in both an A-favouring and a B-favouring mirror (12 unique pairs x 8 repetitions = 96 trials), so side bias cancels exactly.

INTERPRETATION: a graded, margin-monotone function that is IDENTICAL for sparse and dense cells supports Tallying; a margin-monotone function that is systematically shifted upward in the sparse (tie-padded, proportion-1.0) cells relative to the dense cells with the same margin, together with adherence ceilings around 0.70-0.80 at M=3, uniquely supports LSNC and cannot be produced by Tallying under any beta/epsilon.

metric.rationale:
This is the overall adherence rate to the full-tally winner (the option that wins on strictly more features), pooled over the 96 trials of the design (every trial in this design has a non-zero tally margin, so no trial is dropped).

Why it separates the theories: LSNC's core commitment is that only a small, randomly drawn subset of cues (mean k between 1.5 and 3.5 of the 6 features) is ever inspected, that tied cues occupy sampling slots (tie dilution), and that each inspected comparison is mis-registered with probability nu = .12-.32. A small noisy sample frequently reverses or fails to recover the sign of the global margin, so LSNC's adherence is structurally CAPPED: exact enumeration for this design gives ~0.57-0.75 across the six cells, i.e. an aggregate near 0.65-0.68, and it cannot approach 1 for any admissible parameter setting. Tallying, in contrast, reads every feature and passes the exact margin (M = 1, 2 or 3 here, never 0) through a softmax; over the bulk of its inverse-temperature range the softmax is essentially deterministic, so its adherence sits near 1 - epsilon/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.90 on average and never structurally attenuated by the composition of the profile.

This is not trivially true of my theory: Tallying is perfectly free to produce low adherence (small beta, large epsilon), and LSNC is free to produce moderately high adherence (large k, small nu) - the metric measures a behavioural ceiling, not a theory label. The prediction that humans in a 6-cue, feedback-free, high-conflict task fall far short of margin-consistent responding (adherence well below 0.8 even at margin 3) is the substantive LSNC claim; Tallying, which by construction integrates all cues, has to attribute any such shortfall to a degenerate temperature that would then also flatten the margin gradient. The metric is a simple proportion over ~96 trials per subject, so its per-subject sampling noise is small (sd ~0.04-0.05), keeping the between-subject variance tight relative to the ~0.2 mean gap.

    eps = float(min(max(eps, 0.0), 1.0))

    if n == 0:
        return np.ones(2) / 2.0

    # ---- distribution of the inspected sample size K in {1..n} -------------
    if n == 1:
        pK = np.array([1.0])
    else:
        q = (k - 1.0) / (n - 1.0)
        q = float(min(max(q, 0.0), 1.0))
        pK = np.array([comb(n - 1, s - 1) * (q ** (s - 1)) * ((1.0 - q) ** (n - s))
                       for s in range(1, n + 1)], dtype=float)
        tot = pK.sum()
        pK = pK / tot if tot > 0 else np.ones(n) / float(n)

    # ---- exact enumeration over sample compositions ------------------------
    pA = 0.0
    for si, s in enumerate(range(1, n + 1)):
        w = float(pK[si])
        if w <= 0.0:
            continue
        denom = float(comb(n, s))
        for ai in range(0, min(nA, s) + 1):
            for bi in range(0, min(nB, s - ai) + 1):
                ti = s - ai - bi
                if ti < 0 or ti > nT:
                    continue
                cnt = comb(nA, ai) * comb(nB, bi) * comb(nT, ti)
                if cnt == 0:
                    continue
                ph = float(cnt) / denom          # multivariate hypergeometric
                m = ai + bi                      # informative cues in sample
                if m == 0:
                    pA += w * ph * 0.5           # nothing discriminates -> guess
                    continue
                # X = number of sampled comparisons REGISTERED as A-wins
                d1 = np.array([comb(ai, x) * ((1.0 - nu) ** x) * (nu ** (ai - x))
                               for x in range(ai + 1)], dtype=float)
                d2 = np.array([comb(bi, x) * (nu ** x) * ((1.0 - nu) ** (bi - x))
                               for x in range(bi + 1)], dtype=float)
                dist = np.convolve(d1, d2)
                xs = np.arange(m + 1)
                p_win = float(dist[2 * xs > m].sum())
                p_tie = float(dist[2 * xs == m].sum())
                pA += w * ph * (p_win + 0.5 * p_tie)

    pA = float(min(max(pA, 0.0), 1.0))
    p = np.array([pA, 1.0 - pA], dtype=float)
    p = (1.0 - eps) * p + eps * 0.5
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1.0)
    return p / p.sum()
proposer_theory.rationale:
Take-The-Best (pi_1) is falsified in both directions (0.90 vs 0.474; 0.14 vs 0.65) and softmax Tallying (pi_2), while parameter-freely correct at chance on Experiment 1's tally ties, over-predicts conflict-trial adherence (0.85 vs 0.65) because a large raw margin drives its softmax to near-determinism unless beta collapses toward guessing everywhere. LSNC dissolves this tension with a single mechanism.

(1) **Experiment 1 is fit parameter-freely.** On tally-tied, side-counterbalanced profiles nA = nB, and uniform (validity-blind) subset sampling plus symmetric encoding noise make the whole process exchangeable in A/B, so p(A) = 0.5 exactly for every parameter setting. Predicted TTB-agreement = 0.50 (real 0.4738), and the only across-subject variance is binomial (0.25/32 ≈ 0.0078 vs. observed 0.0073) — matching not just the mean but the observed between-subject spread.

(2) **Experiment 2's attenuation falls out mechanically.** The two conflict configurations are (nA=1, nB=4, nT=1) and (nA=1, nB=3, nT=2). Exact enumeration gives adherence to the tally winner of ~0.60 (K=1), ~0.63 (K=2), ~0.67 (K=3) at nu ≈ 0.25, rising only slowly toward 1 as K → n. With the declared ranges (mean k ≈ 2.5, nu ≈ 0.22, eps ≈ 0.06) the pooled prediction is ≈ 0.655, essentially the observed 0.6538, and the parameter spread contributes ≈ 0.002 on top of the 0.007 binomial variance, landing near the observed 0.0092. Crucially, adherence is *capped*: no amount of increasing determinism drives it to 1 unless the sample becomes the full profile, so the model is not merely a re-tuned Tallying.

(3) **It is a genuine rival with a testable dissociation.** Because the subset is drawn from all cues — including tied ones — adherence depends on the *proportion* of informative cues won and is *diluted* by uninformative cues, not on the raw margin M. Note above that the 1-vs-4 (margin 3, one tied cue) and 1-vs-3 (margin 2, two tied cues) cases already differ by ~0.03–0.05 at fixed parameters in a direction Tallying cannot represent; a 2-0 versus 4-2 design (both M=2) yields a large predicted gap under LSNC and none under Tallying. The model uses no validity information at all, honouring the Experiment 1 evidence against validity-ordered or validity-weighted search, and it generalises to any n_features and any validity vector without refitting.

experiment.rationale:
GOAL: dissociate softmax Tallying (advocated) from Limited-Sample Noisy Cue Counting (LSNC, competing). Tallying's choice probability is a function of the tally margin M = nA - nB ALONE: P(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*M) + eps/2. Therefore any two profiles with the same M MUST yield exactly the same P(A) for every beta and epsilon -- a parameter-free invariance. LSNC instead depends on the full composition (nA, nB, nT): because the inspected subset is drawn uniformly from ALL features, tied cues occupy sampling slots (tie dilution) and only the PROPORTION of sampled informative cues won matters, so adherence must fall monotonically as a fixed margin is realized with fewer ties and more loser-wins.

DESIGN: 8 experts, scrambled validity spread [0.93, 0.55, 0.78, 0.86, 0.60, 0.71, 0.66, 0.82] (descending rank f0 > f3 > f7 > f2 > f5 > f6 > f4 > f1, so validity order is decoupled from screen position). 2 (margin: M = 2, 4) x 3 (composition: SPARSE / MID / DENSE) factorial, each cell fully mirrored for side => 12 unique pairs x 8 repetitions ~ 96 trials.

Cells (A-favouring version; mirror swaps A and B):
- S2 sparse M=2: (nA,nB,nT) = (2,0,6)
- M2 mid    M=2: (3,1,4)
- D2 dense  M=2: (5,3,0)
- S4 sparse M=4: (4,0,4)
- M4 mid    M=4: (5,1,2)
- D4 dense  M=4: (6,2,0)

QUANTITATIVE PREDICTIONS. Tallying: a pure margin main effect and EXACTLY ZERO composition effect -- the three M=2 cells must be statistically identical, the three M=4 cells must be statistically identical, and the M=4 level must exceed M=2 by the sigmoid gap sigmoid(4b) - sigmoid(2b). LSNC (exact enumeration, k=2.5, nu=0.20, eps=0): M=2 -> 0.661 (sparse) vs ~0.62 (mid) vs 0.598 (dense); M=4 -> 0.750 (sparse) vs ~0.72 (mid) vs 0.689 (dense). I.e. LSNC predicts a monotone ~6-point decline across the composition ladder at BOTH margins, plus adherence capped near 0.75-0.80 even at M=4. Note that at sample size K=1 all same-margin cells coincide (P = 0.5 + 0.3*M/n), so any composition effect in the data is diagnostic of multi-cue but sub-total sampling; a flat ladder is diagnostic of full integration (Tallying).

CONFOUND CONTROLS. (i) In every A-favouring cell option A wins the highest-validity cue f0 (0.93), which discriminates in all six cells, so Take-The-Best / any 'best cue' rule predicts a CONSTANT P(A) across all cells and cannot generate either the margin effect or a composition ladder. (ii) Validity-weighted additive evidence (log-odds weights) was deliberately matched WITHIN each margin level: M=2 cells give net +2.99 (sparse), +3.04 (mid), +3.12 (dense); M=4 cells give +4.55, +4.78, +4.39. Hence WADD-type integration also predicts no composition effect, so a sparse>mid>dense ordering can only come from sample-limited counting with tie dilution, while a flat ladder plus a clear margin effect uniquely supports Tallying. (iii) Tied cues are encoded sometimes 1-1 and sometimes 0-0 so that display density of 1s is not itself a cue to composition. (iv) Every configuration appears in both an A-favouring and a B-favouring mirror, so side bias cancels exactly.

INTERPRETATION: margin-graded but composition-invariant adherence (with the M=4 cells approaching the ceiling implied by the beta estimated from the M=2 cells) supports Tallying; a systematic sparse > mid > dense decline at each margin, with adherence capped around 0.75 at M=4, supports LSNC.

metric.metric_source:
def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    """Adherence to the full-profile tally winner.

    For every trial we recompute the global feature-wise win counts
    nA = #(A > B) and nB = #(B > A) over ALL features, identify the
    option favoured by the complete tally, and score whether the subject
    chose it. The returned scalar is the proportion of such trials on
    which the subject followed the complete-tally winner.

    Works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on a single subject's
    slice.
    """
    a_col = data['option_a_ratings'].tolist()
    b_col = data['option_b_ratings'].tolist()
    r_col = data['response'].tolist()

    hits = []
    for a_raw, b_raw, r in zip(a_col, b_col, r_col):
        a = np.asarray(a_raw, dtype=float).ravel()
        b = np.asarray(b_raw, dtype=float).ravel()
        if a.shape[0] != b.shape[0] or a.shape[0] == 0:
            continue
        nA = float(np.sum(a > b))
        nB = float(np.sum(b > a))
        if nA == nB:
            continue  # undiagnostic (no complete-tally winner)
        winner = 0 if nA > nB else 1
        try:
            resp = int(r)
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            continue
        if resp not in (0, 1):
            continue
        hits.append(1.0 if resp == winner else 0.0)

    if len(hits) == 0:
        return float('nan')
    return float(np.mean(hits))
metric.rationale:
The single sharpest quantitative divergence between the two accounts is the ATTAINABLE LEVEL of adherence to the complete-profile tally winner on clearly discriminating pairs. Every trial in this design has a strict global tally winner with margin M = 2 or M = 4, and (by construction) the option favoured by the tally also wins the most valid cue, so the metric is not confounded by cue-order strategies.

Under softmax Tallying the decision variable is the FULL margin: P(winner) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*M) + eps/2. Since M >= 2 on every trial, sigmoid(beta*M) is already essentially at ceiling for most of the beta range, so adherence is pinned near 1 - eps/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.90 on average and, crucially, only weakly dispersed (its across-subject spread comes from the lapse parameter alone, since 48 + 48 trials wash out binomial noise).

Under LSNC the inspected subset averages ~2.5 of 8 cues and each comparison is mis-registered with prob nu ~ 0.2, so a large global margin is routinely reversed or diluted by tied cues occupying sampling slots. Exact enumeration for this design gives adherence ~0.60-0.66 at M=2 and ~0.69-0.75 at M=4, i.e. a pooled value around 0.66-0.70 that is CAPPED well below what full integration produces, and again tightly distributed across subjects because the parameter ranges (k in [1.5,3.5], nu in [0.12,0.32]) move it only a few points.

So the expected contrast is roughly 0.87 vs 0.68 with per-subject variances of order 0.005-0.008 in both cases, which at N=25 is a very large Welch t. This is not trivially true of Tallying: had subjects been strongly noise-limited, Tallying's own epsilon/beta would drag adherence down toward the LSNC band; the prediction that adherence sits high above the sample-limited ceiling is a substantive commitment of full-cue integration.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by counting, across all features, how often one option has a higher value than the other. The option that wins on more features is chosen. Tallying discards cardinal magnitudes — only the sign of each feature-wise comparison matters — so the heuristic is robust to monotone rescaling of individual features and cannot be swayed by a single large feature difference in the way Equal-Weight can. Ties on an individual feature contribute nothing to either count: that cue is simply treated as uninformative for the pair. No feature is privileged, in contrast to Take The Best; every cue contributes equally to the tally. When the two counts are equal the heuristic has no basis for preference and the learner must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the two tallies with inverse temperature beta (interpolating between fully deterministic choice at large beta and uniform guessing at beta = 0), plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Tallying heuristic (Dawes 1979; Gigerenzer &
    # Goldstein 1999). Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors
    # for the current trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features),
    # with row 0 = option A, row 1 = option B. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Tallying expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    # Count strict feature-wise wins; ties contribute to neither option.
    a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
    b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
    scores = np.array([a_wins, b_wins])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. When
    # a_wins == b_wins the softmax is exactly uniform regardless of
    # beta, which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating
    # tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

next_theory.description:
**Count-Direction with Conflict-Graded Confidence (CDCC).**

When people compare two multi-attribute options described by binary expert ratings, the *direction* of their preference and the *confidence* with which they execute it are computed by two functionally separate processes.

1. **Direction is purely count-based.** The comparator registers, for each attribute, only which option is rated higher, and the option that wins on more attributes becomes the candidate response. Validities never enter this stage: they cannot promote a minority-supported option to candidate status. When the two win-counts are equal, the comparator returns no candidate at all, and the subject flips a mental coin — exactly 0.5, with **no** validity-ordered tie-break. This is a hard, parameter-free prediction: on tally-tied, side-counterbalanced profiles CDCC predicts chance adherence to the most-valid discriminating cue, regardless of any parameter setting.

2. **Confidence, not direction, carries the validity information, and it is graded by evidence dilution and by cue conflict.** The probability of actually executing the count-winner is a saturating (tanh) function of a scalar confidence signal built from three ingredients: (i) the raw win margin M = |nA − nB|; (ii) *dilution* — the margin is discounted by the total number of discriminating cues raised to a power gamma, so that a 6-vs-2 split feels much weaker than a 4-vs-0 split even though both have M = 4 (evidence spread thin across many mutually contradicting attributes is subjectively less compelling than a clean, sparse, unanimous split); and (iii) *coherence* — the signed, normalised balance of validity weight between the cues the count-winner wins and the cues the loser wins, where the subjective weight of a cue is a convex (super-linear) function of its stated validity advantage, w_j = (v_j − 0.5)^rho. Convexity means the coherence signal is dominated by the few high-validity cues: when the best cue points *with* the count the subject feels certain, when it points *against* the count the subject feels torn even though the count itself is unambiguous.

3. **Conflict erodes confidence but never reverses direction.** The confidence argument is floored at zero, so validity conflict can drive behaviour arbitrarily close to guessing but never below chance: CDCC never makes systematic one-reason (Take-The-Best) choices. This is what separates it from any Tallying+TTB mixture: on high-margin trials where the top cue opposes the tally, people move toward 0.5 from above, not past it.

4. **Lapses.** With probability epsilon the entire decision is replaced by a coin flip (attention lapse), which caps adherence below 1 even on maximally coherent trials.

The theory therefore predicts a specific cross-design signature: chance performance on tally-tied profiles; high but sub-ceiling adherence on sparse, coherent, unanimous profiles; noticeably lower adherence on dense profiles where the loser also wins several cues even when the raw margin is larger; and the lowest (but still above-chance) adherence when the most valid cue opposes the count.
next_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, state, history):
    import numpy as np

    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim == 1:
        stim = stim.reshape(2, -1)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        stim = stim.reshape(2, -1)
    a = stim[0]
    b = stim[1]
    n = int(a.shape[0])

    if n == 0:
        return np.array([0.5, 0.5], dtype=float)

    a_win = a > b
    b_win = b > a
    nA = int(np.sum(a_win))
    nB = int(np.sum(b_win))
    D = nA + nB

    # --- Commitment 1: direction is purely count-based; ties -> exact guess ---
    if D == 0 or nA == nB:
        return np.array([0.5, 0.5], dtype=float)

    winner = 0 if nA > nB else 1
    M = float(abs(nA - nB))

    # --- parameters -----------------------------------------------------
    beta = float(parameters.get("beta", 2.6))
    gamma = float(parameters.get("gamma", 1.5))
    kappa = float(parameters.get("kappa", 0.7))
    rho = float(parameters.get("rho", 3.0))
    eps = float(parameters.get("epsilon", 0.10))

    beta = min(max(beta, 0.0), 20.0)
    gamma = min(max(gamma, 0.0), 3.0)
    kappa = min(max(kappa, 0.0), 5.0)
    rho = min(max(rho, 0.5), 8.0)
    eps = min(max(eps, 0.0), 0.6)

    # --- validity weights (convex in validity advantage) ------------------
    v_raw = parameters.get("validities", None)
    v = None
    if v_raw is not None:
        try:
            v = np.asarray(v_raw, dtype=float).ravel()
        except Exception:
            v = None
    if v is None or v.shape[0] != n:
        # fallback: assume features are ordered by descending validity
        v = np.linspace(0.95, 0.55, n) if n > 1 else np.array([0.75])

    w = np.clip(v - 0.5, 1e-9, None) ** rho

    if winner == 0:
        W_win = float(np.sum(w[a_win]))
        W_lose = float(np.sum(w[b_win]))
    else:
        W_win = float(np.sum(w[b_win]))
        W_lose = float(np.sum(w[a_win]))

    tot = W_win + W_lose
    C = 0.0 if tot <= 0.0 else (W_win - W_lose) / tot   # in [-1, 1]

    # --- Commitment 2: dilution-discounted margin, coherence-gated --------
    S = M / (float(D) ** gamma)
    gate = (1.0 + kappa * C) / (1.0 + kappa)             # 1.0 when fully coherent
    arg = beta * S * gate

    # --- Commitment 3: conflict erodes confidence, never reverses it ------
    if arg < 0.0:
        arg = 0.0
    if arg > 30.0:
        arg = 30.0

    conf = float(np.tanh(arg))

    # --- Commitment 4: lapse ---------------------------------------------
    p_winner = 0.5 + 0.5 * (1.0 - eps) * conf
    p_winner = float(min(max(p_winner, 0.5), 1.0 - 1e-9))

    p = np.empty(2, dtype=float)
    p[winner] = p_winner
    p[1 - winner] = 1.0 - p_winner

    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1.0)
    return p / p.sum()
next_theory.rationale:
Minimal-diff edit on the running-best iter-1 base. The mechanism is left completely untouched: count-only direction, exact parameter-free 0.5 on tally ties, tanh(beta * M/D^gamma * coherence gate), convex weights w=(v-0.5)^rho, chance floor, and the multiplicative lapse. The ONLY change is the epsilon range, shifted slightly downward from [0.02, 0.22] to [0.02, 0.18] (centre 0.12 -> 0.10), plus the matching default in the code.

Why this and nothing else: the critic has now explicitly retracted the dispersion-chasing line of advice, since two consecutive box-widening attempts (three-way widening in iter 2, epsilon-only symmetric widening in iter 3) produced literally zero Exp3/Exp4 between-subject variance gain and both were rejected by the gate. On those coherent, near-saturating trials p_winner is flat over any admissible box, so the residual dispersion is not recoverable in-family and chasing it only perturbs the levels the loss actually rewards. The remaining genuine residuals of the accepted base are level residuals in a single, consistent direction: Exp3 0.776 vs 0.794 (-0.018) and Exp4 0.749 vs 0.755 (-0.006), both LOW.

Epsilon enters strictly linearly and multiplicatively on the confidence term (p = 0.5 + 0.5*(1-eps)*tanh(...)), so lowering its mean by 0.02 raises adherence by ~0.5*0.02*tanh(...) ~= +0.010 uniformly on saturated trials and proportionally less on weak-evidence trials. That lifts Exp3 to ~0.786 and Exp4 to ~0.759, shrinking both residuals, while moving Exp2's conflict cell only ~+0.006 (0.649 -> ~0.655, essentially exactly the observed 0.654 because the coherence gate there is well below saturation so the tanh factor is smaller). Exp1 is untouched by construction: every scored trial is a tally tie, which returns exactly [0.5, 0.5] before any parameter is read, so its residual against 0.474 remains pure simulation sampling noise and is not being tuned against.

Critically the sparse > dense inversion is preserved: gamma, beta, kappa and rho are all identical to the accepted base, so the relative ordering of confidence signals across designs (Exp3's D=1/2/3 sparse splits with S near 1.0-0.58 vs Exp4's dense 5v3/6v2 splits with S near 0.09-0.18) is unchanged; epsilon only rescales the whole confidence curve, keeping Exp3 > Exp4 intact while nudging both toward their targets. This is the smallest edit that reduces two of the three tunable level residuals simultaneously with no risk of the Exp4 overshoot that killed iter 2 (epsilon can only raise adherence toward the target from below, never past the tanh ceiling implied by the fixed beta/gamma).

experiment.rationale:
GOAL: dissociate Limited-Sample Noisy Cue Counting (LSNC, advocated) from Count-Direction with Conflict-Graded Confidence (CDCC, competing). Both theories agree on the count-based DIRECTION of choice and both cap adherence below 1, so the classic tally-vs-TTB contrasts are useless here. They differ on exactly two things, and this design isolates both.

KEY DISSOCIATION 1 (parameter-free for LSNC): COHERENCE. LSNC's predicted probability is a function of the composition (nA, nB, nT) ALONE 
cue identity/validity is irrelevant because the inspected subset is drawn uniformly at random. CDCC's confidence is gated by the coherence term C = (W_win - W_lose)/(W_win + W_lose) with convex weights w = (v-0.5)^rho, so it must show a large drop when the highest-validity cue is won by the count LOSER, holding (nA, nB, nT) exactly fixed. Every composition therefore appears in a COHERENT version (count winner also wins the top-validity cues, loser wins only the weakest ones) and a CONFLICT version (count winner wins only the weakest cues, loser wins the top cue(s)), with the identical (nA, nB, nT).

KEY DISSOCIATION 2 (composition ordering reversal): with n = 6 fixed, CDCC's dilution term is S = M/D^gamma (D = nA+nB, ties irrelevant), whereas LSNC's dilution comes from tied cues occupying sampling slots and from the PROPORTION of sampled informative cues won. These give opposite orderings for two of the three cells: LSNC ranks (4,2,0) ABOVE (2,1,3) (0.630 vs 0.589), while CDCC ranks (2,1,3) ABOVE (4,2,0) (0.633 vs 0.602 averaged over coherence; 0.707 vs 0.651 in the coherent versions), because CDCC penalises D = 6 heavily via D^1.5 while LSNC penalises the 3 tied slots.

DESIGN: 6 experts, scrambled validity spread [0.94, 0.57, 0.86, 0.62, 0.70, 0.78] (descending rank f0 > f2 > f5 > f4 > f3 > f1, so validity rank is decoupled from screen position and positional heuristics cannot mimic validity-based coherence). One very high (0.94) and two low (0.57, 0.62) validities make the convex weighting in CDCC bite hard (w = (v-.5)^3 gives f0 = .085 vs f1 = .0003, a 250:1 ratio). 3 compositions x 2 coherence levels x 2 side mirrors = 12 unique pairs x 8 repetitions = 96 trials.

CELLS (A-favouring version listed; the mirror swaps A and B):
- T1/T2  C1-COHERENT (nA,nB,nT) = (2,1,3): A wins f0(.94), f2(.86); B wins f1(.57); f3,f4,f5 tied.
- T3/T4  C1-CONFLICT (2,1,3): A wins f1(.57), f3(.62); B wins f0(.94); f2,f4,f5 tied.
- T5/T6  C2-COHERENT (3,1,2): A wins f0,f2,f5; B wins f1; f3,f4 tied.
- T7/T8  C2-CONFLICT (3,1,2): A wins f1,f3,f4; B wins f0; f2,f5 tied.
- T9/T10 C3-COHERENT (4,2,0): A wins f0,f2,f4,f5; B wins f1,f3.
- T11/T12 C3-CONFLICT (4,2,0): A wins f1,f3,f4,f5; B wins f0,f2.

QUANTITATIVE PREDICTIONS. LSNC (exact enumeration, k = 2.5, nu = 0.20, eps = 0): P(count winner) = 0.589 for (2,1,3), 0.656 for (3,1,2), 0.630 for (4,2,0) 
 IDENTICAL for the coherent and conflict member of each pair (a strictly zero coherence effect, for every k, nu, eps). CDCC (beta = 2.6, gamma = 1.5, kappa = 0.7, rho = 3.0, eps = 0.10): coherent 0.707 / 0.757 / 0.651 versus conflict 0.544 / 0.576 / 0.553 
 a 10-18 point coherence effect that cannot be switched off (kappa > 0.4 by hypothesis) and that is largest for the sparse (2,1,3) and (3,1,2) cells where the loser's single win is the top expert.

Each subject contributes 48 coherent and 48 conflict trials, so the coherence contrast is estimated within subject with high power. INTERPRETATION: adherence that depends only on the (nA,nB,nT) composition, is flat across the coherence manipulation, and shows the (3,1,2) > (4,2,0) > (2,1,3) ordering with a ceiling near 0.65, uniquely supports LSNC. A systematic coherent > conflict gap (never dropping below 0.5) together with the (3,1,2) > (2,1,3) > (4,2,0) ordering uniquely supports CDCC. Below-chance adherence in the conflict cells would falsify BOTH theories in favour of validity-weighted / one-reason integration, so the design is also self-diagnostic.

CONTROLS: (i) every configuration appears in an A-favouring and a B-favouring mirror, so side bias cancels exactly; (ii) tied cues are encoded sometimes 1-1 and sometimes 0-0 so the number of displayed 1s does not covary with composition; (iii) validity order is scrambled relative to display position; (iv) no pair is degenerate 
 every trial has a strict count winner and every trial requires reading more than one rating.

metric.metric_source:
def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd

    validities = np.array([0.94, 0.57, 0.86, 0.62, 0.70, 0.78], dtype=float)

    coh_hit = 0.0
    coh_n = 0.0
    con_hit = 0.0
    con_n = 0.0

    for a_raw, b_raw, resp in zip(data['option_a_ratings'],
                                  data['option_b_ratings'],
                                  data['response']):
        a = np.asarray(list(a_raw), dtype=float)
        b = np.asarray(list(b_raw), dtype=float)
        n = a.shape[0]
        if n == 0:
            continue
        if validities.shape[0] == n:
            v = validities
        else:
            v = np.linspace(0.95, 0.55, n) if n > 1 else np.array([0.75])

        a_win = a > b
        b_win = b > a
        nA = int(a_win.sum())
        nB = int(b_win.sum())
        if nA == nB:
            continue  # no count winner; excluded
        winner = 0 if nA > nB else 1

        disc = a_win | b_win
        if not disc.any():
            continue
        # highest-validity discriminating cue
        idx = int(np.argmax(np.where(disc, v, -np.inf)))
        top_owner = 0 if a_win[idx] else 1
        coherent = (top_owner == winner)

        try:
            r = int(resp)
        except Exception:
            continue
        hit = 1.0 if r == winner else 0.0

        if coherent:
            coh_hit += hit
            coh_n += 1.0
        else:
            con_hit += hit
            con_n += 1.0

    if coh_n == 0.0 or con_n == 0.0:
        return 0.0
    return float(coh_hit / coh_n - con_hit / con_n)
metric.rationale: The design holds the win-count composition (nA,nB,nT) exactly fixed while flipping whether the highest-validity expert (0.94) sides with or against the count winner. LSNC (advocated) samples cues uniformly at random, so its predicted adherence depends only on (nA,nB,nT) and is mathematically invariant to which cues the winner owns: the coherent-minus-conflict adherence difference is exactly 0 for every parameter setting (k, nu, epsilon). CDCC gates confidence through the convex validity-weighted coherence term C, with kappa >= 0.4 by hypothesis, so it must show a large positive gap (~0.15, i.e. ~0.71 coherent vs ~0.56 conflict). Each subject supplies 48 coherent and 48 conflict trials, so the within-subject difference has SE ~0.10, giving a very tight per-subject estimate and a between-theory separation of many standard errors at N=25. Side mirrors within each cell cancel any side bias, and the coherence label is derived generically (winner owns the most valid discriminating cue), so no trial-index bookkeeping is required.

proposer_theory.description:
**Limited-Sample Noisy Cue Counting (LSNC).** People neither integrate all cues (Tallying) nor consult a single best cue (Take-The-Best). Instead, on each choice they inspect only a *limited, randomly selected subset* of the presented expert ratings, tally feature-wise wins **within that sample only**, and pick the option that is ahead in the sample; a within-sample tie (including a sample containing no discriminating cue) forces a guess.

Three commitments define the theory:
1. **Equal-probability sampling.** The inspected subset is drawn uniformly at random from the whole profile — it is *not* validity-ordered and *not* validity-weighted. Stated validities are too weakly represented to steer the search order, so no cue enjoys priority. Consequently, on globally tally-tied, side-counterbalanced profiles the process is exactly symmetric and choice is 50/50, with no tendency to follow the most valid discriminating cue.
2. **Sample-size limitation with tie dilution.** The number of cues actually inspected, K, is a random variable with mean k < n (implemented as K = 1 + Binomial(n−1, q), so at least one cue is always read). Because the subset is drawn from *all* features, non-discriminating (tied) features occupy sampling slots and dilute the evidence: two profiles with the same raw tally margin M produce different adherence depending on how many uninformative cues pad the profile, and on the proportion (not the raw count) of informative cues won. This is the signature that dissociates LSNC from softmax Tallying, whose predictions depend only on M.
3. **Encoding noise + lapse.** Each inspected feature-wise comparison is registered with the wrong sign with probability nu (attention/encoding noise), and with probability epsilon the whole decision is replaced by a coin flip.

Because a small, noisy sample can easily reverse the sign of a large global margin, adherence to the full-tally winner is *capped well below 1* even on high-margin conflict trials — the systematic attenuation that full Tallying cannot produce without degenerate temperature — while symmetry guarantees exactly chance behaviour on tally-tied pairs.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, state, history):
    import numpy as np
    from math import comb

    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError("LSNC expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape %s." % (stim.shape,))
    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    n = int(a.shape[0])

    nA = int(np.sum(a > b))          # cues on which A wins
    nB = int(np.sum(b > a))          # cues on which B wins
    nT = n - nA - nB                 # uninformative (tied) cues

    k = float(parameters["k"])            # mean number of cues inspected
    nu = float(parameters["nu"])          # per-comparison encoding error
    eps = float(parameters["epsilon"])    # lapse rate
    nu = float(min(max(nu, 0.0), 0.5))
    eps = float(min(max(eps, 0.0), 1.0))

    if n == 0:
        return np.ones(2) / 2.0

    # ---- distribution of the inspected sample size K in {1..n} -------------
    if n == 1:
        pK = np.array([1.0])
    else:
        q = (k - 1.0) / (n - 1.0)
        q = float(min(max(q, 0.0), 1.0))
        pK = np.array([comb(n - 1, s - 1) * (q ** (s - 1)) * ((1.0 - q) ** (n - s))
                       for s in range(1, n + 1)], dtype=float)
        tot = pK.sum()
        pK = pK / tot if tot > 0 else np.ones(n) / float(n)

    # ---- exact enumeration over sample compositions ------------------------
    pA = 0.0
    for si, s in enumerate(range(1, n + 1)):
        w = float(pK[si])
        if w <= 0.0:
            continue
        denom = float(comb(n, s))
        for ai in range(0, min(nA, s) + 1):
            for bi in range(0, min(nB, s - ai) + 1):
                ti = s - ai - bi
                if ti < 0 or ti > nT:
                    continue
                cnt = comb(nA, ai) * comb(nB, bi) * comb(nT, ti)
                if cnt == 0:
                    continue
                ph = float(cnt) / denom          # multivariate hypergeometric
                m = ai + bi                      # informative cues in sample
                if m == 0:
                    pA += w * ph * 0.5           # nothing discriminates -> guess
                    continue
                # X = number of sampled comparisons REGISTERED as A-wins
                d1 = np.array([comb(ai, x) * ((1.0 - nu) ** x) * (nu ** (ai - x))
                               for x in range(ai + 1)], dtype=float)
                d2 = np.array([comb(bi, x) * (nu ** x) * ((1.0 - nu) ** (bi - x))
                               for x in range(bi + 1)], dtype=float)
                dist = np.convolve(d1, d2)
                xs = np.arange(m + 1)
                p_win = float(dist[2 * xs > m].sum())
                p_tie = float(dist[2 * xs == m].sum())
                pA += w * ph * (p_win + 0.5 * p_tie)

    pA = float(min(max(pA, 0.0), 1.0))
    p = np.array([pA, 1.0 - pA], dtype=float)
    p = (1.0 - eps) * p + eps * 0.5
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1.0)
    return p / p.sum()
proposer_theory.rationale:
Take-The-Best (pi_1) is falsified in both directions (0.90 vs 0.474; 0.14 vs 0.65) and softmax Tallying (pi_2), while parameter-freely correct at chance on Experiment 1's tally ties, over-predicts conflict-trial adherence (0.85 vs 0.65) because a large raw margin drives its softmax to near-determinism unless beta collapses toward guessing everywhere. LSNC dissolves this tension with a single mechanism.

(1) **Experiment 1 is fit parameter-freely.** On tally-tied, side-counterbalanced profiles nA = nB, and uniform (validity-blind) subset sampling plus symmetric encoding noise make the whole process exchangeable in A/B, so p(A) = 0.5 exactly for every parameter setting. Predicted TTB-agreement = 0.50 (real 0.4738), and the only across-subject variance is binomial (0.25/32 ≈ 0.0078 vs. observed 0.0073) — matching not just the mean but the observed between-subject spread.

(2) **Experiment 2's attenuation falls out mechanically.** The two conflict configurations are (nA=1, nB=4, nT=1) and (nA=1, nB=3, nT=2). Exact enumeration gives adherence to the tally winner of ~0.60 (K=1), ~0.63 (K=2), ~0.67 (K=3) at nu ≈ 0.25, rising only slowly toward 1 as K → n. With the declared ranges (mean k ≈ 2.5, nu ≈ 0.22, eps ≈ 0.06) the pooled prediction is ≈ 0.655, essentially the observed 0.6538, and the parameter spread contributes ≈ 0.002 on top of the 0.007 binomial variance, landing near the observed 0.0092. Crucially, adherence is *capped*: no amount of increasing determinism drives it to 1 unless the sample becomes the full profile, so the model is not merely a re-tuned Tallying.

(3) **It is a genuine rival with a testable dissociation.** Because the subset is drawn from all cues — including tied ones — adherence depends on the *proportion* of informative cues won and is *diluted* by uninformative cues, not on the raw margin M. Note above that the 1-vs-4 (margin 3, one tied cue) and 1-vs-3 (margin 2, two tied cues) cases already differ by ~0.03–0.05 at fixed parameters in a direction Tallying cannot represent; a 2-0 versus 4-2 design (both M=2) yields a large predicted gap under LSNC and none under Tallying. The model uses no validity information at all, honouring the Experiment 1 evidence against validity-ordered or validity-weighted search, and it generalises to any n_features and any validity vector without refitting.

experiment.rationale:
GOAL: dissociate Count-Direction with Conflict-Graded Confidence (CDCC, advocated) from Limited-Sample Noisy Cue Counting (LSNC, competing). Both theories agree that the DIRECTION of choice is the count winner and both cap adherence below 1, so tally-vs-TTB style contrasts are useless. They differ on exactly what modulates adherence: LSNC's probability is a function of the composition (nA, nB, nT) ALONE (uniform sampling makes cue identity/validity irrelevant), whereas CDCC's confidence is (i) gated by validity COHERENCE C = (W_win - W_lose)/(W_win + W_lose) with convex weights w = (v-0.5)^rho, and (ii) diluted by S = M/D^gamma where D = nA+nB, so tied cues are completely irrelevant to CDCC but occupy sampling slots for LSNC. This design attacks both differences and, crucially, contains two ORDERING REVERSALS.

DESIGN: 7 experts, scrambled validity spread [0.94, 0.58, 0.86, 0.63, 0.72, 0.80, 0.55] (descending rank f0 > f2 > f5 > f4 > f3 > f1 > f6, so validity rank is decoupled from screen position and positional heuristics cannot mimic validity coherence). One very high (0.94) and two very low (0.58, 0.55) validities make the convex weighting bite: w = (v-.5)^3 gives f0 = .0852 vs f6 = .000125, a ~680:1 ratio. 6 configurations x 2 side mirrors = 12 unique pairs x 8 repetitions = 96 trials.

CELLS (A-favouring version listed; the even-numbered mirror swaps A and B):
- T1/T2  SPARSE-COHERENT (nA,nB,nT) = (2,1,4): A wins f0(.94), f2(.86); B wins f6(.55); rest tied.
- T3/T4  SPARSE-CONFLICT  (2,1,4): A wins f1(.58), f6(.55); B wins f0(.94); rest tied. IDENTICAL composition to T1/T2.
- T5/T6  DENSE-COHERENT   (4,2,1): A wins f0,f2,f5,f4; B wins f3,f1; f6 tied.
- T7/T8  DENSE-CONFLICT   (4,2,1): A wins f1,f3,f4,f6; B wins f0,f2; f5 tied. IDENTICAL composition to T5/T6.
- T9/T10 UNANIMOUS-SPARSE (2,0,5): A wins f2,f4; five tied cues, no cue opposes.
- T11/T12 UNANIMOUS-DENSE (4,0,3): A wins f0,f3,f5,f6; three tied cues, no cue opposes.

QUANTITATIVE PREDICTIONS.
CDCC (beta=2.6, gamma=1.5, kappa=0.7, rho=3.0, eps=0.10): (2,1,4) coherent 0.708 vs conflict 0.541; (4,2,1) coherent 0.651 vs conflict 0.540; (2,0,5) 0.928; (4,0,3) 0.888.
LSNC (exact enumeration, k=2.5, nu=0.20, eps=0): (2,1,4) 0.579 for BOTH coherent and conflict; (4,2,1) 0.621 for BOTH; (2,0,5) 0.680; (4,0,3) 0.770.

THREE ORTHOGONAL DIAGNOSTICS:
(1) COHERENCE (parameter-free for LSNC): holding (nA,nB,nT) exactly fixed, CDCC predicts a 11-17 point coherent-minus-conflict gap that cannot be switched off (kappa >= 0.4 by hypothesis), while LSNC predicts EXACTLY ZERO for every k, nu, epsilon. Each subject contributes 32 coherent and 32 conflict trials on matched compositions, so this contrast is estimated within subject with high power.
(2) SPARSITY REVERSAL among the coherent cells: CDCC's D^gamma dilution makes (2,1,4) [D=2 winners vs 1 loser, D=3] MORE confident than (4,2,1) [D=6] despite the smaller raw margin (0.708 > 0.651); LSNC's tie dilution predicts the OPPOSITE order (0.579 < 0.621) because the sparse cell wastes 4 of 7 sampling slots on tied cues. Same reversal for the unanimous cells: CDCC predicts (2,0,5) > (4,0,3) (0.928 > 0.888, and 0.911 > 0.826 at gamma=1.75), LSNC predicts (4,0,3) > (2,0,5) (0.770 > 0.680). A margin-2 profile beating a margin-4 profile is impossible for LSNC under any parameters.
(3) CEILING: on the clean unanimous-sparse cell CDCC allows 0.90-0.95 adherence, whereas LSNC is capped near 0.68 (and at most ~0.79 even at k=3.5, nu=0.12) because a small noisy sample easily reverses the sign. Adherence above ~0.85 on T9/T10 is outside LSNC's reachable range.

CONTROLS: (i) every configuration appears in an A-favouring and a B-favouring mirror, so side bias cancels exactly; (ii) tied cues are encoded sometimes 1-1 and sometimes 0-0 so the number of displayed 1s does not covary with composition or coherence; (iii) validity rank is scrambled relative to display position; (iv) no pair is degenerate: every trial has a strict count winner and requires reading several ratings; (v) systematic BELOW-chance adherence in the conflict cells (i.e. following the single best cue against the tally) would falsify BOTH theories in favour of one-reason/WADD integration, so the design is self-diagnostic.

INTERPRETATION: a large coherent > conflict gap that never dips below 0.5, together with sparse > dense ordering at matched or even smaller margins and near-0.9 adherence on unanimous sparse profiles, uniquely supports CDCC. Flat adherence across the coherence manipulation with a (4,0,3) > (2,0,5) > (4,2,1) > (2,1,4) composition ordering and a ceiling near 0.7 uniquely supports LSNC.

metric.rationale:
Two structurally signed contrasts are summed, each of which has an opposite (or null) sign under the two theories, so the composite separates them with a large mean gap while each component is estimated from 32/32 and 16/16 trials per subject (tight per-subject noise).

D1 = adherence(count-winner) on validity-COHERENT conflicting profiles minus adherence on validity-INCOHERENT profiles, with the (nA,nB,nT) composition held EXACTLY matched across the two sets by design (T1/T2 vs T3/T4 both (2,1,4); T5/T6 vs T7/T8 both (4,2,1)). LSNC samples cues uniformly and ignores validity entirely, so its predicted adherence depends only on (nA,nB,nT): D1 = 0 exactly, for every k, nu, epsilon. CDCC gates confidence by the convex validity-weighted coherence C, so D1 is strictly positive (~+0.11 to +0.17, larger for larger kappa) and cannot be turned off.

D2 = adherence on the UNANIMOUS-SPARSE profile (2 winning cues, 0 opposing, 5 tied) minus adherence on the UNANIMOUS-DENSE profile (4 winning cues, 0 opposing, 3 tied). For CDCC the dilution term S = M/D^gamma gives 2^(1-gamma) vs 4^(1-gamma) = (2^(1-gamma))^2, and since gamma > 1 the sparse profile ALWAYS yields the larger confidence: D2 >= 0 for every admissible parameter vector. For LSNC tied cues waste sampling slots, so the dense profile (4/7 informative slots) always beats the sparse one (2/7): D2 < 0 (~ -0.06 to -0.12) for every admissible parameter vector.

Hence the composite D1 + D2 is bounded below by 0 under CDCC (expected ~ +0.18) and is expected to be clearly negative under LSNC (~ -0.09), a gap of roughly 0.27 with per-subject variance dominated by binomial sampling over 96 trials (sd ~ 0.17), which gives a Welch t well above 4 at N=25. It is not trivially true for CDCC: a flat coherence effect or an ordering with dense > sparse on unanimous profiles would push the metric to zero/negative and falsify it.

proposer_theory.description:
**Count-Direction with Conflict-Graded Confidence (CDCC).**

When people compare two multi-attribute options described by binary expert ratings, the *direction* of their preference and the *confidence* with which they execute it are computed by two functionally separate processes.

1. **Direction is purely count-based.** The comparator registers, for each attribute, only which option is rated higher, and the option that wins on more attributes becomes the candidate response. Validities never enter this stage: they cannot promote a minority-supported option to candidate status. When the two win-counts are equal, the comparator returns no candidate at all, and the subject flips a mental coin — exactly 0.5, with **no** validity-ordered tie-break. This is a hard, parameter-free prediction: on tally-tied, side-counterbalanced profiles CDCC predicts chance adherence to the most-valid discriminating cue, regardless of any parameter setting.

2. **Confidence, not direction, carries the validity information, and it is graded by evidence dilution and by cue conflict.** The probability of actually executing the count-winner is a saturating (tanh) function of a scalar confidence signal built from three ingredients: (i) the raw win margin M = |nA − nB|; (ii) *dilution* — the margin is discounted by the total number of discriminating cues raised to a power gamma, so that a 6-vs-2 split feels much weaker than a 4-vs-0 split even though both have M = 4 (evidence spread thin across many mutually contradicting attributes is subjectively less compelling than a clean, sparse, unanimous split); and (iii) *coherence* — the signed, normalised balance of validity weight between the cues the count-winner wins and the cues the loser wins, where the subjective weight of a cue is a convex (super-linear) function of its stated validity advantage, w_j = (v_j − 0.5)^rho. Convexity means the coherence signal is dominated by the few high-validity cues: when the best cue points *with* the count the subject feels certain, when it points *against* the count the subject feels torn even though the count itself is unambiguous.

3. **Conflict erodes confidence but never reverses direction.** The confidence argument is floored at zero, so validity conflict can drive behaviour arbitrarily close to guessing but never below chance: CDCC never makes systematic one-reason (Take-The-Best) choices. This is what separates it from any Tallying+TTB mixture: on high-margin trials where the top cue opposes the tally, people move toward 0.5 from above, not past it.

4. **Lapses.** With probability epsilon the entire decision is replaced by a coin flip (attention lapse), which caps adherence below 1 even on maximally coherent trials.

The theory therefore predicts a specific cross-design signature: chance performance on tally-tied profiles; high but sub-ceiling adherence on sparse, coherent, unanimous profiles; noticeably lower adherence on dense profiles where the loser also wins several cues even when the raw margin is larger; and the lowest (but still above-chance) adherence when the most valid cue opposes the count.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, state, history):
    import numpy as np

    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim == 1:
        stim = stim.reshape(2, -1)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        stim = stim.reshape(2, -1)
    a = stim[0]
    b = stim[1]
    n = int(a.shape[0])

    if n == 0:
        return np.array([0.5, 0.5], dtype=float)

    a_win = a > b
    b_win = b > a
    nA = int(np.sum(a_win))
    nB = int(np.sum(b_win))
    D = nA + nB

    # --- Commitment 1: direction is purely count-based; ties -> exact guess ---
    if D == 0 or nA == nB:
        return np.array([0.5, 0.5], dtype=float)

    winner = 0 if nA > nB else 1
    M = float(abs(nA - nB))

    # --- parameters -----------------------------------------------------
    beta = float(parameters.get("beta", 2.6))
    gamma = float(parameters.get("gamma", 1.5))
    kappa = float(parameters.get("kappa", 0.7))
    rho = float(parameters.get("rho", 3.0))
    eps = float(parameters.get("epsilon", 0.10))

    beta = min(max(beta, 0.0), 20.0)
    gamma = min(max(gamma, 0.0), 3.0)
    kappa = min(max(kappa, 0.0), 5.0)
    rho = min(max(rho, 0.5), 8.0)
    eps = min(max(eps, 0.0), 0.6)

    # --- validity weights (convex in validity advantage) ------------------
    v_raw = parameters.get("validities", None)
    v = None
    if v_raw is not None:
        try:
            v = np.asarray(v_raw, dtype=float).ravel()
        except Exception:
            v = None
    if v is None or v.shape[0] != n:
        # fallback: assume features are ordered by descending validity
        v = np.linspace(0.95, 0.55, n) if n > 1 else np.array([0.75])

    w = np.clip(v - 0.5, 1e-9, None) ** rho

    if winner == 0:
        W_win = float(np.sum(w[a_win]))
        W_lose = float(np.sum(w[b_win]))
    else:
        W_win = float(np.sum(w[b_win]))
        W_lose = float(np.sum(w[a_win]))

    tot = W_win + W_lose
    C = 0.0 if tot <= 0.0 else (W_win - W_lose) / tot   # in [-1, 1]

    # --- Commitment 2: dilution-discounted margin, coherence-gated --------
    S = M / (float(D) ** gamma)
    gate = (1.0 + kappa * C) / (1.0 + kappa)             # 1.0 when fully coherent
    arg = beta * S * gate

    # --- Commitment 3: conflict erodes confidence, never reverses it ------
    if arg < 0.0:
        arg = 0.0
    if arg > 30.0:
        arg = 30.0

    conf = float(np.tanh(arg))

    # --- Commitment 4: lapse ---------------------------------------------
    p_winner = 0.5 + 0.5 * (1.0 - eps) * conf
    p_winner = float(min(max(p_winner, 0.5), 1.0 - 1e-9))

    p = np.empty(2, dtype=float)
    p[winner] = p_winner
    p[1 - winner] = 1.0 - p_winner

    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1.0)
    return p / p.sum()
proposer_theory.rationale:
Minimal-diff edit on the running-best iter-1 base. The mechanism is left completely untouched: count-only direction, exact parameter-free 0.5 on tally ties, tanh(beta * M/D^gamma * coherence gate), convex weights w=(v-0.5)^rho, chance floor, and the multiplicative lapse. The ONLY change is the epsilon range, shifted slightly downward from [0.02, 0.22] to [0.02, 0.18] (centre 0.12 -> 0.10), plus the matching default in the code.

Why this and nothing else: the critic has now explicitly retracted the dispersion-chasing line of advice, since two consecutive box-widening attempts (three-way widening in iter 2, epsilon-only symmetric widening in iter 3) produced literally zero Exp3/Exp4 between-subject variance gain and both were rejected by the gate. On those coherent, near-saturating trials p_winner is flat over any admissible box, so the residual dispersion is not recoverable in-family and chasing it only perturbs the levels the loss actually rewards. The remaining genuine residuals of the accepted base are level residuals in a single, consistent direction: Exp3 0.776 vs 0.794 (-0.018) and Exp4 0.749 vs 0.755 (-0.006), both LOW.

Epsilon enters strictly linearly and multiplicatively on the confidence term (p = 0.5 + 0.5*(1-eps)*tanh(...)), so lowering its mean by 0.02 raises adherence by ~0.5*0.02*tanh(...) ~= +0.010 uniformly on saturated trials and proportionally less on weak-evidence trials. That lifts Exp3 to ~0.786 and Exp4 to ~0.759, shrinking both residuals, while moving Exp2's conflict cell only ~+0.006 (0.649 -> ~0.655, essentially exactly the observed 0.654 because the coherence gate there is well below saturation so the tanh factor is smaller). Exp1 is untouched by construction: every scored trial is a tally tie, which returns exactly [0.5, 0.5] before any parameter is read, so its residual against 0.474 remains pure simulation sampling noise and is not being tuned against.

Critically the sparse > dense inversion is preserved: gamma, beta, kappa and rho are all identical to the accepted base, so the relative ordering of confidence signals across designs (Exp3's D=1/2/3 sparse splits with S near 1.0-0.58 vs Exp4's dense 5v3/6v2 splits with S near 0.09-0.18) is unchanged; epsilon only rescales the whole confidence curve, keeping Exp3 > Exp4 intact while nudging both toward their targets. This is the smallest edit that reduces two of the three tunable level residuals simultaneously with no risk of the Exp4 overshoot that killed iter 2 (epsilon can only raise adherence toward the target from below, never past the tanh ceiling implied by the fixed beta/gamma).

next_theory.description:
**Redundancy-Discounted Tiered Integration with Majority Discounting, Panel-Size Capacity Dilution, and Graded Redundancy Relaxation (RDTI-MCR).**

All previous commitments are retained. (i) Stated validities are encoded only *coarsely and ordinally*: a median split into a "star" tier and a "marginal" tier, with no gradations inside a tier. (ii) The star tier is treated as **redundant** — the very accurate experts are construed as merely restating the obvious consensus quality of the product — so their ratings enter integration with only a small residual weight, while the idiosyncratic marginal experts carry full weight. Evidence is the tier-weighted signed sum E = Σ_j w_j (a_j − b_j), and choice is logistic in that scalar plus an attention lapse. Because the weights take only two values, tier-matched profiles cancel *exactly* and give an exact coin flip, with no validity tie-break and no take-the-best fallback. (iii) The same redundancy logic is applied to the majority itself: a feature-count majority is the most "obvious" statistic in the display, so subjects apply a *contrarian consensus discount* proportional to the count margin. (iv) Integration is capacity-limited over the *whole displayed panel*, so the effective slope is divided by a power of the panel size n, in addition to a milder within-trial spread discount over the number of discriminating cues D.

**The new commitment is that the redundancy discount is itself a comparative, graded judgement rather than a fixed property of a cue.** A star expert is discounted precisely *because other experts are seen as restating what he says*; the discount is therefore a function of how much of the panel is actually speaking on this trial. When almost nothing in the display discriminates — in the limit, when a single expert is the only one who differentiates the two products — there is no chorus for that expert to be redundant with, so his rating is taken at (nearly) full face value.
